newsitem.title: UK: Merck says Ecu drug price aim is fair access.
newsitem.headline: Merck says Ecu drug price aim is fair access.

text.p: International drugs giant Merck & Co Inc said on Friday its decision to price a new AIDS drug in European currency units (Ecus) uniformly across the European Union was aimed at ensuring fair access to the drug for all.
The EU earlier approved Merck's anti-HIV and AIDS drug Crixivan, the first ever drug to be priced using the Ecu for sale across its 15 member states.
The U.S. company is also breaking with the standard practice in the industry of setting different prices for drugs sold to individual countries.

Merck spokesman Jeffrey Sturchio told Reuters it was concerned that price distortions across the EU, where each country fixes its own drug prices, might deprive some patients of continued access to the drug.

Huge variations in pricing within the EU lead to the widespread practice of parallel importing of drugs, with products re-exported from lower priced countries, notably Spain and Portugal, to undercut the same product elsewhere.

Sturchio said the practice "can lead to problems with stocks running out in some countries and too much in others. We were trying to think of a way that we could minimise disruption in Europe and ensure fair and equal distribution."

But in a telephone interview he also said that Merck saw the move as setting a precedent for future drug launches in Europe as it pushes for the creation of a genuine single market for pharmaceuticals.

"It is so important that patients have continual access (to Crixivan) and we were mainly concerned with that, but secondly we wanted to endorse the move to the single market and the single currency," he said.

He said Crixivan, which is used in combination with other drugs, lowered levels of the HIV virus in the blood "to almost negligible levels". But if treatment is halted, the virus could develop resistance, "so it is important that patients that start on Crixivan are maintained on it."
Merck's unilateral move on pricing, however, is not as dramatic as it first appears. All it can do is charge a uniform price, in this case 9.64 Ecus a day, for the product which leaves its factories.
But widely varying national price rules, distribution costs, taxation and currency fluctutations will continue to distort the price charged for Crixivan in individual markets.
Merck said it had not spoken to other companies about the move but hoped that they would take an interest in what Merck was doing.
A spokesman for rival SmithKline Beecham Plc said a uniform price across the EU "could act as a disincentive for parallel importing" but added this was not something the company had looked at.
